summary: A description of the Telnet logger and server for the CP/CMS system on the Lincoln Laboratory 360/67, listed as host 10. It serves half and full duplex users with ASCII or EBCDIC data, uses the hide-input and no-echo controls during login, and follows the initial connection protocol. The text says it was not cleared for public release.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 466 describes a TELNET logger and server for Lincoln Laboratory's CP/CMS system. It explains its character conversion, login handling, and support for different terminal modes.

subtitle: How the Lincoln Laboratory CP/CMS TELNET logger and server worked.

tldr.problem: The Lincoln Laboratory CP/CMS system needed a TELNET service for users with ASCII or EBCDIC data and half- or full-duplex terminals.
tldr.mechanism: A logger sets up connections and a server translates between network ASCII, EBCDIC, and TELNET control codes.
tldr.outcome: The RFC documents the implementation, including login handling, line buffering, and the stated limit of three simultaneous users.

today: The unit metadata lists RFC 466's status as Unknown. The RFC documents a TELNET implementation for a specific CP/CMS host.

sections.title: The Lincoln Laboratory TELNET Service
sections.content:
RFC 466 documents the TELNET logger/server for CP/CMS on Lincoln Laboratory's 360/67, identified as host 10. It supports half-duplex and full-duplex users and data in ASCII or EBCDIC codes.

The RFC says the material was not reviewed for public release and was intended only for ARPA Network use.
sections.plainLanguage: The service let network users connect to Lincoln Laboratory's CP/CMS computer. It supported two character codes and two ways of handling input and output.

sections.title: Starting a Session and Logging In
sections.content:
The logger follows the initial connection protocol and chooses a pair of TELNET sockets after an initial request. It refuses a new connection when its current limit of three users is reached.

After connection, the logger identifies ASCII or EBCDIC operation. During login, TELNET hide-your-input and noecho controls map to CP/CMS print-suppression and restore functions; a file provides network passwords corresponding to CP passwords.
sections.plainLanguage: The logger establishes the TELNET connections and determines which character code to use. During login, special controls hide password input and restore normal printing.

sections.title: Translation and Line-Based Input
sections.content:
The server translates incoming ASCII into EBCDIC for CP/CMS and maps output back to network ASCII when a mapping exists. It also maps TELNET controls such as hide-your-input, noecho, and break to EBCDIC codes or system actions.

CP/CMS processes input one line at a time, so the server buffers characters until a newline. The TELNET break control also serves as an end-of-message signal and, for half-duplex users, an input prompt.
sections.plainLanguage: The server changes incoming characters into the form CP/CMS expects and translates output back. It waits for a complete line before processing input.
